content: Your doctor has prescribed heparin, a medication that works as an anticoagulant to thin your blood. This is intended to prevent the formation of blood clots in your body. Additionally, heparin may be used to stop existing blood clots from growing larger. The medication will be administered either intravenously (directly into a vein) or subcutaneously (under the skin). Your doctor will determine the most appropriate dosing schedule for your condition. Intravenous administration may last for 1 to 2 weeks, while subcutaneous injections could continue for up to 6 weeks or even 6 months. In some cases, heparin may be prescribed for other medical purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist if you need further clarification. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and check for side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your body responds to the medication. Before starting heparin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have any allergies to heparin, pork products, or other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and over-the-counter medications you are currently taking, including aspirin, ibuprofen (Motrin), naproxen (Anaprox, Aleve), headache or pain medications, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney disease or diabetes. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, let your doctor know. Should you become pregnant while on heparin, contact your doctor immediately. Before administering heparin, inspect the solution carefully. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. Follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. If this happens, contact your provider immediately to resume therapy as soon as possible. Heparin may cause side effects, the most common of which is excessive bleeding (hemorrhage). If you experience any of the following symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately: Bleeding from the gums or nose Unusually heavy menstrual bleeding Excessive bleeding from cuts or wounds Easy bruising Purplish discoloration on the skin Blood in your urine or stools Vomiting or coughing up blood Chills Fever Itching Rash If you experience a severe side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of heparin and provide instructions for proper storage. Store the medication in a cool, clean, and dry area, ensuring it does not freeze. Follow your provider’s directions for storage carefully. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injuries. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving heparin through a vein or under the skin, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection, which can occur at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you notice any of the following symptoms near the catheter site: Tenderness Warmth Irritation Drainage Redness Swelling Pain
